events.title: Re-Leaf Agency
events.description: A Multisensory Performance Prompting Reflection and Action Re-Leaf Agency invites you into an immersive environment of lush movement, rich sounds, provocative text, and larger-than-life video projections of trees, mushrooms, ferns, wildflowers, and streams spanning multiple surfaces. The performers summon you into the woods, amplifying all manner of small and precious flora and fauna, to reveal a needed refuge. Re-Leaf Agency is a recruitment session disguised as a performance, or maybe it’s a performance disguised as a recruitment session. Either way, this is the last time in 2026 when you can join the Agency to become a keeper of the good. Three Re-Leaf Agents - two dancers and a recruitment officer - implore you to join them in navigating the turbulent times in which we find ourselves. Amidst the anxiety of an unraveling democracy and the impacts of a changing climate, Re-Leaf Agency rekindles hope by taking the long view of the natural world. This multimedia piece is the culmination of several years documenting a sliver of earth on the edge of Maryland’s South Mountain, during which time MAD Dance director Kit Clark experienced the solace of non-human time while walking and witnessing the land. Re-Leaf Agency shares that profound experience with others. Dancers Amanda Comi and Jeanna Riscigno join Clark in this one-of-a-kind performance.

events.description: 8 performances | Oct. 31 and Nov. 6*, 7, 13 & 14 at 7:30 p.m. | Nov. 1, 8 & 15 at 2 p.m. Set in one of the most pivotal times in America’s history, the Tony-nominated Caroline, or Change is riveting, moving, and awe-inspiring. Featuring a virtuosic score by Jeanine Tesori (Shrek The Musical, Thoroughly Modern Millie), it blends blues, gospel and traditional Jewish melodies, creating a breathtaking medium for Kushner’s provocative and personal story. In 1963, the Gellman family and their African-American maid, Caroline, live in sleepy Lake Charles, Louisiana. Caroline is drifting through life as a single mother of four, working in a service job for a white family. A fragile, yet beautiful friendship develops between the young Gellman son, Noah, and Caroline. Noah’s stepmother, Rose, unable to give Caroline a raise, tells Caroline that she may keep the money that Noah leaves in his pockets. Caroline balks and refuses to take money from a child, but her own children desperately need food, clothing and shoes. Outside of the laundry room, some of the greatest social advancements that the country has seen are being set in motion, and change is knocking on the door. Caroline, or Change, produces a valuable theatrical experience that continues to thrill audiences the world over. It is a story that must be shared and will touch hearts. events.title: Tapping into Timelessness - $45
events.description: Who hasn’t counted down the days to an upcoming vacation, waiting for the fun to begin? But what if we didn’t have to wait for a break from everyday life to experience deeper presence, connection, and joy? We spend much of our lives organizing ourselves around time—watching the clock, managing schedules, meeting deadlines, and trying to fit more into already-full days. Yet we also experience moments when our usual relationship with time seems to disappear. We become absorbed in something we love, deeply connected, or fully present to the moment. What if we could experience more of life not by cramming more into our time, but by changing how we inhabit it? In this experiential workshop, we’ll consider how our state of consciousness can shape our experience of time. Through discussion, reflection, and guided meditation, we’ll reconnect with moments of timelessness, explore what allows us to move beyond ordinary “clock time,” and discover how shifting our state of being can transform everyday experiences. Ultimately, you will leave with intentions for tapping into timelessness more intentionally and creating more space for the experiences that bring richness, meaning, and joy to your life.

events.title: The Legend of Sleepy Hollow-Olney Theatre
events.description: Olney audiences were blown away in 2025, when we invited Synetic Theater to perform their award-winning, wordless version of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream . Now they’re back, but this time they’re tackling a story with classic American roots in the intimate confines of Olney Theatre Center’s 150-seat Theatre Lab. In the haunted village of Sleepy Hollow, the past refuses to stay buried. Years after a brutal Revolutionary War encounter leaves a Hessian soldier beheaded and his beloved horse slain, the fallen rider returns as the legendary Headless Horseman—an apparition stalking the shadowed forests in search of what was taken from him. Inspired by Washington Irving’s classic tale, Sleepy Hollow reimagines the familiar legend as a haunting story of love, guilt, revenge, and redemption. Blending supernatural horror with theatrical spectacle, it asks whether the true monsters are the spirits who haunt us—or the deeds we would rather forget. By Washington Irving Adapted by Nathan Weinberger Directed by Paata Tsikurishvili Choreographed by Irina Tsikurishvili Due to the layout of the Mulitz-Gudelsky Theatre Lab, late seating is at the discretion of the House Manager. Those exiting the theatre during the performance will not be re-admitted while the performance is in progress.

events.title: Camp One Heartland
events.description: Camp One Heartland is a solo exhibition by Tye DuSold-O’Connor archiving documentation of one of the world’s first nonprofit summer camps designated to supporting and empowering youth affected by HIV and AIDS, eventually transforming into a vital beacon of safety, liberation and eutopia for LGBTQ+ youth across the country. After its inaugural session in the summer of 1993 and many more held at different campsites across the country, Camp One Heartland found its permanent residence in Willow River, Minnesota. Over the next three decades it broadened its reach to provide summer camp sessions for youth experiencing housing instability, LGBTQ+ youth, and specifically trans youth. Tye attended Camp One Heartland as both a camper in 2022 and a counselor in 2024, and found these experiences indescribably transformative to them and their queer identity. Quite suddenly, Camp One Heartland shut down permanently in the fall of 2024 due to financial issues. Former campers, counselors and staff have been unable to return to the site since. While camp counseling in the summer of 2024, Tye took hundreds of photos of the camp, its people, and its experiences. These serve as some of the last images taken during the lifetime of Camp One Heartland. We also recognize the people, resources, and everyday actions that help us uphold our commitment to integrity, accountability, and excellence in truth and service. 5 ways to participate in Compliance Week: 1. Curated by Kathryn Coney-Ali, executive director of the Howard University Gallery of Art, and Dr. Melanee C. Harvey-Fryar, associate professor of art history in the Chadwick A. Boseman College of Fine Arts, the exhibition brings Waheed’s documentary street photography into conversation with selections from the Waheed Photo Archive. Together, the works explore Black joy, protest, community, cultural tradition, and the power created when people gather. Necessary Means opens Wednesday, October 14, 2026, at the Howard University Museum in Founders Library and remains on view through May 28, 2027.

events.title: Research & Enrichment! Science with Your Dog
events.description: Join the GW Dog Lab for fun, free enrichment with your dog! The GW Canine Cognition Collaborative (aka GW Dog Lab) is a student-run lab in the Anthropology Department. Research sessions are on campus, after hours and on weekends, and are designed to last only 1 hour. Because humans and dogs share an environment, we can learn a lot about the way that environment has shaped our species by comparing dog and toddler cognition. We play simple games with dogs designed to measure their cognition and then compare them to toddlers. How to Participate 1. Start by submitting a pre-screening form. This helps us learn about your dog 2. Next, open your email and look for your onboarding information sent from canine.cognition@gwu.edu. 3. Then, using the information in your email, sign up for your initial visit. This is a get-to-know-you visit that makes it easier for dogs to get acclimated to our testing space. 4. Finally, after the initial visit, depending on your dog's comfort level, you will get email invitations to studies your dog is eligible for! Parking information can be found on the GW Dog Lab website.

events.title: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power
events.description: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power, an exhibition examining the beauty, dynamism, and political force of collective Black life across the African Diaspora through the photography of Howard alumna Adreinne Waheed. Curated by Kathryn Coney-Ali, executive director of the Howard University Gallery of Art, and Dr. Melanee C. Harvey-Fryar, associate professor of art history in the Chadwick A. Boseman College of Fine Arts, the exhibition brings Waheed’s documentary street photography into conversation with selections from the Waheed Photo Archive. Together, the works explore Black joy, protest, community, cultural tradition, and the power created when people gather. Necessary Means opens Wednesday, October 14, 2026, at the Howard University Museum in Founders Library and remains on view through May 28, 2027.

events.title: West Asia: A New American Grand Strategy in the Middle East
events.description: Attend In-Person Attend Online Please join the Middle East Policy Forum, in partnership with the Sigur Center for Asian Studies, on November 3 to welcome Mohammed Soliman, author of West Asia: A New American Grand Strategy in the Middle East. Dr. Alyssa Ayres, Dean of the Elliott School of International Affairs, will deliver opening remarks. Mohammed Soliman argues in his book that it is time for the United States to move decisively away from nation-building and get back to the business of order-building. To do so will require zooming out, in both geographical and historical terms, to build a new regional order across ‘West Asia’ – from the Middle East to South Asia, connecting Europe to the Indo-Pacific via the Mediterranean and Red Seas. Working with India, Italy, Greece, France, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Japan, the UK, and the United Arab Emirates, among others, he shows how the United States could lock in a new balance of power in the Eurasian supercontinent to offset Chinese and Russian efforts to disrupt the status quo and create a rival system. This new strategy rests on three layered coalitions — geostrategic, hard-power, and geo-technological — that together can anchor a stable order stretching from the Mediterranean to the Indian Ocean. But this will require a fundamental shift in U.S. grand strategy, with ‘West Asia’ at its core. All are invited to this Middle East Policy Forum event, cosponsored by the Sigur Center for Asian Studies and moderated by Ambassador (ret.) G

events.title: Who Killed Alex Odeh? Film Screening
events.description: In October 1985, Santa Ana, California, was shaken by a brazen act of political violence when a Palestinian American, Alex Odeh, a beloved teacher and community leader, was killed by a tripwire bomb planted in his office. Despite clear evidence and identified suspects, the case was never solved. Who Killed Alex Odeh? reopens the mystery, tracking a renewed investigation in real time as new leads emerge, long-buried records come to light, and the forces behind a political assassination are finally confronted. Unfolding like a detective thriller, the film weaves archival footage, firsthand testimony, and new reporting to expose the violent fundamentalist networks behind the attack and the institutional failures that protected them. As the investigation deepens, the story widens to reveal how the extremist ideology that fueled Odeh’s murder did not disappear - it evolved, gaining traction and legitimacy in the modern political landscape. Directed by SMPA Professors Jason Osder and William Lafi Youmans, a Jewish American and a Palestinian American, Who Killed Alex Odeh? is both a gripping cold-case pursuit and a timely examination of political violence, asking what it means when acts of terror go unresolved, and how justice denied continues to shape the world we live. The screening will be held on November 3 at 6 p.m. in the MPA 5th Floor Studio.

events.description: A multidisciplinary showcase from the artists and scholars of the full-time faculty and staff at the Corcoran School of the Arts & Design. A Gift In Motion loosely draws from Robin Wall Kimmerer’s book The Serviceberry which uplifts Indigenous frameworks of the natural world to advance the possibilities in collectivity, reciprocity, and the mindset of abundance. These are anti-capitalist models and theories that provide insight into the systems of power we negotiate, but also offer a lens on how we individually move through our daily lives—together—through historically fraught landscapes. A keen reminder that working with, for, and because of each other remains the most human motivation, even while we are inundated with narratives that suggest otherwise. Within the walls of the academy, frameworks of artistic and creative knowledge are often dismissed, as are Indigenous methodologies and community-focused perspectives that center human engagement, oral and craft-based practices, and unquantifiable research. A personal experience. A feeling. Abstraction. And yet, for centuries, within the walls of art schools exist myriad economies of imagination that are anchored in the sharing of diverse creative knowledge and articulated in what we make, write, perform, dance, build, conserve, collect, display, speak, and think. events.title: BME Department Seminar
events.description: Join the Department of Biomedical Engineering for their upcoming seminar featuring Dr. Simiao Niu, an assistant professor at Rutgers University! He will be presenting "Battery-free Wireless Bioelectronic Network for Effective Chronic Disease Management." Abstract: 60% of the US population live with at least one chronic disease. These diseases and associated comorbidities are now the leading causes of death. Effective management of complex chronic diseases requires body-wide, long-term, accurate, and continuous monitoring of multiple physiological signals from wearable devices to precisely determine the pathological state. These wearable physiological signal monitoring can dramatically reduce the demand of physician visiting and increase patients’ engagement and treatment adherence rate. Although wearable bioelectronic devices have shown huge potential in chronic disease management, existing technology still mostly relies on rigid chip components, where the interface between chips and skin/tissue has been a bottleneck that limits the system performance (noise, robustness etc). To address these challenges, my group's research has been involved in the exploration of rational system design concepts, material and device fabrication innovation, tailored algorithms, and energy harvesting to enable a closed-loop wireless bioelectronic network that targets next-generation chronic disease management. In this talk, I will discuss my group's efforts in building this technology platform.

events.title: Camp One Heartland
events.description: Camp One Heartland is a solo exhibition by Tye DuSold-O’Connor archiving documentation of one of the world’s first nonprofit summer camps designated to supporting and empowering youth affected by HIV and AIDS, eventually transforming into a vital beacon of safety, liberation and eutopia for LGBTQ+ youth across the country. After its inaugural session in the summer of 1993 and many more held at different campsites across the country, Camp One Heartland found its permanent residence in Willow River, Minnesota. Over the next three decades it broadened its reach to provide summer camp sessions for youth experiencing housing instability, LGBTQ+ youth, and specifically trans youth. Tye attended Camp One Heartland as both a camper in 2022 and a counselor in 2024, and found these experiences indescribably transformative to them and their queer identity. Quite suddenly, Camp One Heartland shut down permanently in the fall of 2024 due to financial issues. Former campers, counselors and staff have been unable to return to the site since. While camp counseling in the summer of 2024, Tye took hundreds of photos of the camp, its people, and its experiences. These serve as some of the last images taken during the lifetime of Camp One Heartland. Artist Bio: Tye DuSold-O’Connor is a multimedia artist studying Fine Art and Psychology whose work revolves around trans experience, identity and culture. events.title: Cannupa Hanska Luger’s REFLECT
events.description: REFLECT traces the evolution of artist Cannuap Hanska Luger’s Mirror Shield Project. In 2016, when the Dakota Access Pipeline threatened the waters of his ancestral homelands, Luger circulated a video demonstrating how to make “mirror shields” from inexpensive materials. Conceived during the Indigenous-led resistance at Standing Rock, North Dakota, the tutorial functioned as a call to collective action, an invitation for people across the country to stand in solidarity with the Water Protectors. Carried by Water Protectors in frontline actions and collective formations, the mirrored surfaces offered protection while redirecting the field of vision. More than a thousand mirror shields were created and transported to the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ camp. The exhibition brings the project’s history into the present, treating the archive as a resource to be carried forward and put into practice. Photographs, videos, garments, ephemera, and community-generated documentation reveal a collective artwork shaped by those who made, carried, adapted, interpreted, and activated it.

events.title: Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection
events.description: The 1920s emerged as a decade suspended between collapse and reconstruction, an era marked by “cracks and reforms” that ushered in a profound reconfiguration of the visual world. During this period marked by civil transformation and political upheaval, artists, journalists, and makers had opportunities to reconstruct both individual and collective identities. A century later, Cracks & Reforms presents a distinct cross-section of this period, revealing global currents of migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition through the lens of the GW Collection. Students led by Associate Professor Bibiana Obler selected works to study and exhibit, their research eventually leading to unified themes and a catalog designed by Corcoran graphic design students led by professors Sharmila Karamchandani and Aasawari Kulkarni. Image: Boris Ignatovich (Russian, 1899-1976), Composer Dmitri Shostakovich, from "Ignatovich, Soviet Avant-Garde", 1928, gelatin silver print, 16 H x 20 W in. events.title: Demo-ing, Sampling, Lip-Syncing: Commercial Misogynoir in Post-Disco EDM
events.description: Join the GW Women's, Gender, and Sexuality Studies (WGSS) Program for an exciting talk from Visiting Assistant Professor Eva Pensis! Across the late 20th century, the popular music industry faced a series of scandals in live performance with the widespread use of lip-syncing. Following the advent of recorded sound, the commercial use of lip-sync in the popular music industry sought to divide the recorded performance from the performer with the aim of controlling both, most often eliding the visual presence of African American musicians while profiting from their sonic contributions. Framed by the media theorist Moya Bailey's concept of "misogynoir," this presentation considers the case of Black Box, an Italian post-disco house music band from the 1980s who stole and misattributed the vocal demos of Martha Wash (a noted musician and vocalist from The Weather Girls and Two Tons o’ Fun) for their debut album. The ensuing crisis of representation that lip-syncing indexes forms the basis for this talk's investigation into the popular music industry's predation on African American women's song following the infamous demolition of disco and the digital quest to strip sound from song. RSVP online.

events.title: Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY
events.description: For Freedoms presents artist and educator Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY which centers on Ethiopian journalist and author Baalu Girma’s controversial 1984 Amharic novel Oromay, written under the Derg regime and banned shortly after its publication. Drawing on Gottesman’s deep engagement with the novel, NIGHT AND DAY considers how artists create, communicate, and sustain cultural memory within and against conditions of censorship, political repression, and state violence. The exhibition extends beyond the gallery through a library of banned books, a self-guided workshop station that invites visitors to respond to censorship through writing and drawing, and a public conversation on how artists sustain creative practice amid sociopolitical pressure.

Humanities in Asia: Going Beyond Make-Do-the Reshaping of a Chinese Operatic Tradition in Taiwan
events.description: Kunqu, a 600-year-old form of Chinese opera known for its poetic lyrics and refined singing, was among the first Chinese art forms UNESCO recognized as a "Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity" in 2001. The story of how Kunqu survived the political upheavals of the twentieth century runs not only through state-sponsored troupes in China but also through communities of devoted amateur singers, known as quyou (曲友), who carried the tradition to Taiwan. This talk follows these enthusiasts from their roots in Mainland China to their postwar lives in Taiwan, where they kept Kunqu alive through informal singing gatherings long before it was celebrated as world heritage. When cultural exchanges across the Taiwan Strait reopened, amateurs and professionals on both sides began collaborating on performances, training, preservation, and documentation, turning a private pastime into a shared project of heritage-making. Drawing on the experiences of Taiwan-based practitioners, the talk shows how this cross-strait collaboration reshaped Kunqu as a heritage for Sinophone audiences and how a common love for an art form built networks that reached beyond politics while still raising questions about cultural identity. Free lunch will be offered at this talk. Doors will open no sooner than 15 minutes before the start time. events.description: At November’s Symposium, we turn to the courts. Judges, lawyers, and the Department of Justice all serve as checks on executive power, and during this Symposia on Government Oversight and Accountability we will examine how that role is shifting. We’ll consider what the mid-term elections mean for judicial oversight, what recent Supreme Court opinions have decided and what they signal going forward, how the DOJ is changing, and how judges are responding to the Administration’s actions in court. events.description: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power, an exhibition examining the beauty, dynamism, and political force of collective Black life across the African Diaspora through the photography of Howard alumna Adreinne Waheed. Curated by Kathryn Coney-Ali, executive director of the Howard University Gallery of Art, and Dr. Melanee C. Harvey-Fryar, associate professor of art history in the Chadwick A. Boseman College of Fine Arts, the exhibition brings Waheed’s documentary street photography into conversation with selections from the Waheed Photo Archive. Together, the works explore Black joy, protest, community, cultural tradition, and the power created when people gather. Necessary Means opens Wednesday, October 14, 2026, at the Howard University Museum in Founders Library and remains on view through May 28, 2027.

events.title: Unfossilizing African Art
events.description: Presented after extensive research, this exhibition recontextualizes African material culture objects held in the GW Collection for nearly 50 years. Led by Assistant Professor Clement Akpang, 59 students from four seminar courses offered between Fall 2024 and Spring 2026, conducted original research to deepen understanding of the university’s holdings and update how we interpret and exhibit these objects. The exhibition features 37 tangible heritage objects, ranging from an Egúngún Paaka from Yorubaland to a Kii [brass pipe], attributed to the Baumum people of Cameroon, accompanied by images and video that illuminate their rich histories. Research on the entire collection is presented in an accompanying illustrated publication. events.title: A Gift in Motion
events.description: A multidisciplinary showcase from the artists and scholars of the full-time faculty and staff at the Corcoran School of the Arts & Design. A Gift In Motion loosely draws from Robin Wall Kimmerer’s book The Serviceberry which uplifts Indigenous frameworks of the natural world to advance the possibilities in collectivity, reciprocity, and the mindset of abundance. These are anti-capitalist models and theories that provide insight into the systems of power we negotiate, but also offer a lens on how we individually move through our daily lives—together—through historically fraught landscapes. A keen reminder that working with, for, and because of each other remains the most human motivation, even while we are inundated with narratives that suggest otherwise. Within the walls of the academy, frameworks of artistic and creative knowledge are often dismissed, as are Indigenous methodologies and community-focused perspectives that center human engagement, oral and craft-based practices, and unquantifiable research. A personal experience. A feeling. Abstraction. And yet, for centuries, within the walls of art schools exist myriad economies of imagination that are anchored in the sharing of diverse creative knowledge and articulated in what we make, write, perform, dance, build, conserve, collect, display, speak, and think. events.title: Camp One Heartland
events.description: Camp One Heartland is a solo exhibition by Tye DuSold-O’Connor archiving documentation of one of the world’s first nonprofit summer camps designated to supporting and empowering youth affected by HIV and AIDS, eventually transforming into a vital beacon of safety, liberation and eutopia for LGBTQ+ youth across the country. After its inaugural session in the summer of 1993 and many more held at different campsites across the country, Camp One Heartland found its permanent residence in Willow River, Minnesota. Over the next three decades it broadened its reach to provide summer camp sessions for youth experiencing housing instability, LGBTQ+ youth, and specifically trans youth. Tye attended Camp One Heartland as both a camper in 2022 and a counselor in 2024, and found these experiences indescribably transformative to them and their queer identity. Quite suddenly, Camp One Heartland shut down permanently in the fall of 2024 due to financial issues. Former campers, counselors and staff have been unable to return to the site since. While camp counseling in the summer of 2024, Tye took hundreds of photos of the camp, its people, and its experiences. These serve as some of the last images taken during the lifetime of Camp One Heartland. Artist Bio: Tye DuSold-O’Connor is a multimedia artist studying Fine Art and Psychology whose work revolves around trans experience, identity and culture. events.title: Cannupa Hanska Luger’s REFLECT
events.description: REFLECT traces the evolution of artist Cannuap Hanska Luger’s Mirror Shield Project. In 2016, when the Dakota Access Pipeline threatened the waters of his ancestral homelands, Luger circulated a video demonstrating how to make “mirror shields” from inexpensive materials. Conceived during the Indigenous-led resistance at Standing Rock, North Dakota, the tutorial functioned as a call to collective action, an invitation for people across the country to stand in solidarity with the Water Protectors. Carried by Water Protectors in frontline actions and collective formations, the mirrored surfaces offered protection while redirecting the field of vision. More than a thousand mirror shields were created and transported to the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ camp. The exhibition brings the project’s history into the present, treating the archive as a resource to be carried forward and put into practice. Photographs, videos, garments, ephemera, and community-generated documentation reveal a collective artwork shaped by those who made, carried, adapted, interpreted, and activated it.

events.title: Courage, Leadership, and Lessons from the Front Lines
events.description: Join us for an engaging discussion about leadership, service, and what it takes to remain steadfast when the stakes are at their highest. Join us for a compelling conversation with Steven Sund, author of Courage Under Fire, and Renn Cannon, author of Eyes on the Rose City, as they share firsthand insights from careers spent navigating some of the most challenging moments in law enforcement, public safety, and national security. Drawing from their books and professional experiences, Sund and Cannon will discuss leadership under pressure, decision-making in uncertain and rapidly evolving situations, and the personal and professional challenges that come with serving in high-stakes environments. They will also explore the importance of preparation, resilience, accountability, and courage when circumstances demand difficult decisions. They will also discuss why education must be a continuing commitment, not just a one-time milestone. In high-stakes professions, leaders and practitioners must continually study evolving threats, examine lessons from critical incidents, challenge assumptions, and translate experience into stronger judgement, preparedness, and decision-making. The webinar will offer students, professionals, and anyone interested in homeland security and public safety an opportunity to hear directly from two experienced practitioners and authors. events.title: Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection
events.description: The 1920s emerged as a decade suspended between collapse and reconstruction, an era marked by “cracks and reforms” that ushered in a profound reconfiguration of the visual world. During this period marked by civil transformation and political upheaval, artists, journalists, and makers had opportunities to reconstruct both individual and collective identities. A century later, Cracks & Reforms presents a distinct cross-section of this period, revealing global currents of migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition through the lens of the GW Collection. Students led by Associate Professor Bibiana Obler selected works to study and exhibit, their research eventually leading to unified themes and a catalog designed by Corcoran graphic design students led by professors Sharmila Karamchandani and Aasawari Kulkarni. Image: Boris Ignatovich (Russian, 1899-1976), Composer Dmitri Shostakovich, from "Ignatovich, Soviet Avant-Garde", 1928, gelatin silver print, 16 H x 20 W in. events.description: High Tea with the Highlands: A Bridgerton-Inspired Tea Party + Highland Cow + Lamb Affair ​ ​Dearest Gentle Readers, It would appear that the ladies of Scarlet Springs Farm have once again orchestrated an affair most enchanting. If you enjoy the Bridgerton series, this is an outing you most certainly won't want to miss as you are most cordially invited to step into a world of romance, refinement, and a touch of pastoral intrigue.​ This two-hour group experience begins, as all great stories should, with an introduction to the true nobility of the countryside—our beloved Highland cows , each most appropriately named after the illustrious Bridgerton family. Spend 30 delightful minutes meeting, petting, brushing, and doting on Penelope and Eloise, tending to Hyacinth and Daphne, and positively swooning over the ever-dashing Benedict. And lest one think the excitement ends there, Simon, Colin, and Alfie—accompanied by their charming entourage of Valais Blacknose and Babydoll lambs—shall also be awaiting your acquaintance, eagerly accepting cuddles, treats, and no small measure of admiration. ​Following your audience with the Highlands, guests will gather for a proper full tea service , thoughtfully prepared and styled for an elegant yet whimsical afternoon. Expect a locally-sourced loose-leaf hot tea accompanied by a classic tea fare prix-fix menu with items such as: Radish and butter tea sandwiches Deviled egg Carrot salad sandwiches Chicken salad tea sandwiches Cucumber tea sandwiches Turkey with cranberry tea sandwiches Fall-flavored scones served with clotted cream and jam Buttermilk biscuits A variety of sweet treats, fit for the ton. (Exact selections may vary by chef.)​ Perfectly suited for couples, a girls’ day out, or a charming mommy & me experience, High Tea with the Highlands promises laughter, indulgence, and memories worthy of society’s highest praise. One can only assume tickets will be in great demand. Yours most sincerely, Lady Whistledown​ ​ $99 per adu

events.title: Mental Reset: Sound Bath + Reiki : Thursday Evenings in Falls Church
events.address: 7777 Leesburg Pike, Ste 204S, Falls Church, VA 22043
events.description: Thursday is a weird day. The week isn't over, but you are. Mental Reset is one hour at the end of the workday where nobody needs anything from you. You come in, you lie down on a mat, you get a blanket and a bolster, and for the next sixty minutes your only job is to listen. I play crystal singing bowls, guide you through a short meditation so your mind has something to do besides replay the day, and offer Reiki while you rest. Most people tell me some version of the same thing afterward: the noise in their head finally turned down. Not off: down. Enough that they can go home and actually be home, instead of answering emails in their head at the dinner table. You don't need experience. You don't need to know how to meditate, and you definitely don't need to “clear your mind.” If you could do that, you wouldn't need this class. First-timers are in the room most weeks. There are ten spots. That's deliberate. It's a small room, I can see everyone in it, and it never feels like an event. It feels like an exhale. A few regulars started as skeptics; more than one of our Google reviews comes from someone who arrived doubting the whole thing and left surprised at how settled they felt. You don't have to believe in anything for an hour of sound and rest to do you some good. Run by Victoria Vita: CPA for 20+ years, healer for 7+. I sat behind a desk with a brain that wouldn't switch off for a long time before I found this work. Thursday nights are built for the person I used to be. Rated 5.0 from 32 Google reviews. Come straight from work. Leave like the week let go of you first. What's included: • 60 minutes of crystal singing bowls, guided meditation and Reiki • Mat, blanket, and bolster everything is here; you bring nothing • Small group: 10 people maximum, same teacher every week • Time at the end to sit up slowly, have water, and not rush out Discover More Attractions in #FXVA

events.title: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power
events.description: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power, an exhibition examining the beauty, dynamism, and political force of collective Black life across the African Diaspora through the photography of Howard alumna Adreinne Waheed. Curated by Kathryn Coney-Ali, executive director of the Howard University Gallery of Art, and Dr. Melanee C. Harvey-Fryar, associate professor of art history in the Chadwick A. Boseman College of Fine Arts, the exhibition brings Waheed’s documentary street photography into conversation with selections from the Waheed Photo Archive. Together, the works explore Black joy, protest, community, cultural tradition, and the power created when people gather. Necessary Means opens Wednesday, October 14, 2026, at the Howard University Museum in Founders Library and remains on view through May 28, 2027.

Directed by Stefan Sittig, a multi-disciplined theatre veteran with 140+ productions across New York City, international venues, and D.C.-area theaters, the production features Sittig's expertise as a Helen Hayes Award-nominated director, choreographer, and fight director. events.title: Research & Enrichment! Science with Your Dog
events.description: Join the GW Dog Lab for fun, free enrichment with your dog! The GW Canine Cognition Collaborative (aka GW Dog Lab) is a student-run lab in the Anthropology Department. Research sessions are on campus, after hours and on weekends, and are designed to last only 1 hour. Because humans and dogs share an environment, we can learn a lot about the way that environment has shaped our species by comparing dog and toddler cognition. We play simple games with dogs designed to measure their cognition and then compare them to toddlers. How to Participate 1. Start by submitting a pre-screening form. This helps us learn about your dog 2. Next, open your email and look for your onboarding information sent from canine.cognition@gwu.edu. 3. Then, using the information in your email, sign up for your initial visit. This is a get-to-know-you visit that makes it easier for dogs to get acclimated to our testing space. 4. Finally, after the initial visit, depending on your dog's comfort level, you will get email invitations to studies your dog is eligible for! Parking information can be found on the GW Dog Lab website.

events.description: SEIZED Film Screening & Discussion SEIZED is a gripping, stranger-than-fiction investigative film that plunges audiences inside the troubling police raid on the Marion County Record. What begins as a shocking small-town incident quickly spirals into a national story, exposing how corruption, politics, and decades-long tensions turned a quaint Kansas community into a battleground over the First and Fourth Amendments. Blending the juicy intrigue of a classic muckraking narrative with a clear-eyed exploration of power, politics, and the fragility of a free press, SEIZED transforms a headline-grabbing event into a deeply human story that is urgent, unsettling, and impossible to ignore. The screening will be followed by a discussion and Q&A featuring the film director, Sharon Liese, and others. Location: Friedman Family Auditorium (Planet Word Museum) Cost: Free View Tickets & More Info

events.title: Unfossilizing African Art
events.description: Presented after extensive research, this exhibition recontextualizes African material culture objects held in the GW Collection for nearly 50 years. Led by Assistant Professor Clement Akpang, 59 students from four seminar courses offered between Fall 2024 and Spring 2026, conducted original research to deepen understanding of the university’s holdings and update how we interpret and exhibit these objects. The exhibition features 37 tangible heritage objects, ranging from an Egúngún Paaka from Yorubaland to a Kii [brass pipe], attributed to the Baumum people of Cameroon, accompanied by images and video that illuminate their rich histories. Research on the entire collection is presented in an accompanying illustrated publication. Image: Once Known Mende carver [Mende, Sierra Leone], Sowei, 19th-20th century, wood, varnish, 16 H x 10 W x 10 D in. Gift of Stephen A. Spear, 1975 (P.75.2.30)

events.description: Join Historic Annapolis for a delightful day trip to Brandywine Museum of Art! You’ll enjoy a guided tour of the Brandywine Museum of Art, followed by a visit to the historic N.C. Wyeth House & Studio. Discover a distinguished collection of nineteenth- and twentieth-century American art, housed in a renovated nineteenth-century mill with a dramatic steel and glass addition that overlooks the bucolic Brandywine River. In 1911, artist N.C. Wyeth used proceeds from his Treasure Island illustrations to buy 18 acres near Chadds Ford, Pennsylvania. Today, the preserved house and studio feature original props, a large mural, and period furnishings that offer a glimpse into Wyeth’s work and family life. The day also includes a delicious lunch and free time to stroll through the beautiful gardens, galleries or browse the museum gift shop. Reserve your seat today—space is limited! Advance registration required; space is limited. Recommended for ages 16+. Cost : $175 General Admission. $160 for HA Members, Volunteers, and Military. Registration is now closed! events.title: A Gift in Motion
events.description: A multidisciplinary showcase from the artists and scholars of the full-time faculty and staff at the Corcoran School of the Arts & Design. A Gift In Motion loosely draws from Robin Wall Kimmerer’s book The Serviceberry which uplifts Indigenous frameworks of the natural world to advance the possibilities in collectivity, reciprocity, and the mindset of abundance. These are anti-capitalist models and theories that provide insight into the systems of power we negotiate, but also offer a lens on how we individually move through our daily lives—together—through historically fraught landscapes. A keen reminder that working with, for, and because of each other remains the most human motivation, even while we are inundated with narratives that suggest otherwise. Within the walls of the academy, frameworks of artistic and creative knowledge are often dismissed, as are Indigenous methodologies and community-focused perspectives that center human engagement, oral and craft-based practices, and unquantifiable research. A personal experience. A feeling. Abstraction. And yet, for centuries, within the walls of art schools exist myriad economies of imagination that are anchored in the sharing of diverse creative knowledge and articulated in what we make, write, perform, dance, build, conserve, collect, display, speak, and think. events.title: Annapolis Jazz & Roots Festival
events.description: Annapolis Jazz & Roots is launching its fifth festival on the scenic shores of the Chesapeake Bay. Events combine music, art, poetry and history on two weekends, November 6-15. Based in the maritime community of Eastport, the festival includes eight venues in nearby neighborhoods. Each has its own distinct character and charm. Festival goers can visit centuries old buildings, take in restorative bay views and stroll the tree-lined streets of the historic Maryland city. THEME AND HIGHLIGHTS The 2026 theme “New World Music: Centuries of Sound” will be brought home by international and regional performers. An adventurous lineup includes programs rooted in history and culture from colonial days to modern times. Trace the evolution of music and culture since the days Indigenous tribes walked the forests and rode the waters. Gain new insights into the startling history and legacy of slavery and indenture in Maryland; delve into the soulful roots of jazz, and celebrate the changing color of sound in America. Events are free or require modest admission, and all but two venues offer free onsite parking. Reservations are strongly advised for all events. Tickets are sold through instantseats.com. WEEKEND ONE Opening Night takes place Friday, November 6 at 7:00 p.m. at St. Luke’s Episcopal Church in Eastport. Jazz lovers will appreciate how the intimacy and beautiful acoustics of the venue elevate the listening experience when the Muneer Nasser Band performs. Trumpeter Muneer Nasser was exposed to great music by his father, jazz bassist Jamil Nasser. This concert pays homage to three legendary musicians born in 1926: John Coltrane, Miles Davis and Randy Weston. Their brave explorations led to seismic shifts in the sonic landscape and continue to resonate around the globe. On Saturday at 11:00 a.m. visit Eastport-Annapolis Neck Library to gain new insights into slavery and indenture in colonial times. Led by Assistant Professor Clement Akpang, 59 students across four seminar courses conducted original research to deepen understanding of the collection and reconsider how these objects are interpreted and exhibited. Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection examines a decade shaped by political upheaval, social transformation, migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition. This exhibition, developed as part of an art history class taught by Associate Professor Bibi Obler, is accompanied by a catalog designed by graphic design students.

His sophomore album, Ultrapure (2023), produced by GRAMMY® winner Daniel Tashian, showcased his raw and earnest exploration of human emotion. Following Ultrapure, Maroney embarked on an extensive world tour, selling out headline shows across North America and Europe while appearing at festivals including Lollapalooza, Osheaga, and All Things Go. In May 2025, he released his acclaimed third studio album, Jimmy, before hitting the road on the expansive Long Hair, Long Life co-headline tour with Peach Pit, his biggest run of shows to date. In 2026, Maroney teamed up with flipturn for a collaborative covers project, further showcasing his versatility as an artist. With new music on the horizon, Briston continues to evolve while building a passionate global fanbase and cementing his place as one of indie music’s most exciting artists.

events.title: Cannupa Hanska Luger’s REFLECT
events.description: REFLECT traces the evolution of artist Cannuap Hanska Luger’s Mirror Shield Project. In 2016, when the Dakota Access Pipeline threatened the waters of his ancestral homelands, Luger circulated a video demonstrating how to make “mirror shields” from inexpensive materials. Conceived during the Indigenous-led resistance at Standing Rock, North Dakota, the tutorial functioned as a call to collective action, an invitation for people across the country to stand in solidarity with the Water Protectors. Carried by Water Protectors in frontline actions and collective formations, the mirrored surfaces offered protection while redirecting the field of vision. More than a thousand mirror shields were created and transported to the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ camp. The exhibition brings the project’s history into the present, treating the archive as a resource to be carried forward and put into practice. Photographs, videos, garments, ephemera, and community-generated documentation reveal a collective artwork shaped by those who made, carried, adapted, interpreted, and activated it.

events.title: Caroline, or Change the Musical
events.description: 8 performances | October 31 and November 6*, 7, 13, and 14 at 7:30pm | November 1, 8, and 15 at 2:00pm *Friday, November 6 will include ASL interpretation and free tickets for Montgomery County residents! Full information at www.r-m-t.org/caroline-or-change Set in one of the most pivotal times in America’s history, the Tony-nominated Caroline, or Change is riveting, moving and awe-inspiring. Featuring a virtuosic score by Jeanine Tesori (Shrek The Musical, Thoroughly Modern Millie), it blends blues, gospel and traditional Jewish melodies, creating a breathtaking medium for Kushner’s provocative and personal story. ​ In 1963, the Gellman family and their African-American maid, Caroline, live in sleepy Lake Charles, Louisiana. Caroline is drifting through life as a single mother of four working in a service job to a white family. A fragile, yet beautiful friendship develops between the young Gellman son, Noah, and Caroline. Noah’s stepmother, Rose, unable to give Caroline a raise, tells Caroline that she may keep the money that Noah leaves in his pockets. Caroline balks and refuses to take money from a child but her own children desperately need food, clothing and shoes. Outside of the laundry room, some of the greatest social advancements that the country has seen are being set in motion, and change is knocking on the door. ​ Caroline, or Change is a story that must be shared and will touch hearts. It is a story that will open minds. It is a story that will change theatergoers

events.description: Carsie Blanton Carsie Blanton is a songwriter with hooks, chutzpah, and revolutionary optimism. Blanton and her road-tested band deploy humor, camaraderie, and considerable musical muscle to enroll each audience in a rare vision of hope and solidarity. In addition to writing and performing music, Carsie works as a political organizer and activist. Soon after, Blanton released The Little Flame, a song of solidarity covered widely on social media during her detention. The Little Flame features background vocals from Irish band Ye Vagabonds and Carsie’s Palestinian/New Zealander prison-mate Rana Hamida, and appears on her latest album, The Red Album Vol II. events.title: Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection
events.description: The 1920s emerged as a decade suspended between collapse and reconstruction, an era marked by “cracks and reforms” that ushered in a profound reconfiguration of the visual world. During this period marked by civil transformation and political upheaval, artists, journalists, and makers had opportunities to reconstruct both individual and collective identities. A century later, Cracks & Reforms presents a distinct cross-section of this period, revealing global currents of migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition through the lens of the GW Collection. Students led by Associate Professor Bibiana Obler selected works to study and exhibit, their research eventually leading to unified themes and a catalog designed by Corcoran graphic design students led by professors Sharmila Karamchandani and Aasawari Kulkarni. Image: Boris Ignatovich (Russian, 1899-1976), Composer Dmitri Shostakovich, from "Ignatovich, Soviet Avant-Garde", 1928, gelatin silver print, 16 H x 20 W in. events.title: Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY
events.description: For Freedoms presents artist and educator Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY which centers on Ethiopian journalist and author Baalu Girma’s controversial 1984 Amharic novel Oromay, written under the Derg regime and banned shortly after its publication. Drawing on Gottesman’s deep engagement with the novel, NIGHT AND DAY considers how artists create, communicate, and sustain cultural memory within and against conditions of censorship, political repression, and state violence. The exhibition extends beyond the gallery through a library of banned books, a self-guided workshop station that invites visitors to respond to censorship through writing and drawing, and a public conversation on how artists sustain creative practice amid sociopolitical pressure.

events.title: Forces of Nature with violinist Francesca Anderegg
events.venue: Maryland Hall for the Creative Arts
events.description: ANNAPOLIS SYMPHONY ORCHESTRA FORCES OF NATURE Friday, November 6, 2026 Saturday, November 7, 2026 6:30 PM Pre Concert Lecture 7:30 PM Concert At Maryland Hall MUSIC PROGRAM Luke Soneral An Overture: The Mouse and its Shadow Reinaldo Moya Vestido de Mar, with violinist Francesca Anderegg Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky The Tempest, Op. 18 Igor Stravinsky Divertimento from Le baiser de la fée (The Fairy’s Kiss) This concert is approximately 2 hours in length, with a 20 minute intermission. In Forces of Nature, the natural world becomes a source of wonder, reflection, and transformation. Emerging composer Luke Soneral opens the program with An Overture: The Mouse and Its Shadow, offering an exciting glimpse of orchestral music’s future. Reinaldo Moya’s ocean-inspired violin concerto, Vestido de Mar, brings violinist Francesca Anderegg to the stage for a work that reflects the landscapes and experiences of the Americas. Tchaikovsky’s The Tempest turns Shakespeare’s storm into a powerful exploration of human nature, while Stravinsky’s The Fairy’s Kiss honors Tchaikovsky through the wintry world of Hans Christian Andersen. Together, these works reveal nature as both an elemental force and a mirror of our inner lives.

events.title: From Consuming to Contributing: How We Built the Space That Was Missing
events.description: Hear from GW Engineering alumnus, Saquib Saifee, M.S. '23, at OWASP Global AppSec USA in San Fransciso, CA! On November 6, he, Caroline Lee, and Gaurang Deshpande from IBM will be leading the panel, "From Consuming to Contributing: How We Built the Space That Was Missing." Many of us naturally drift from consuming OWASP resources to contributing to them. At some point, you stop just reading the Top 10 and start showing up at a chapter, submitting a pull request, or volunteering at a conference. But what often gets lost is the "together" part. The shared strategy, the mutual encouragement, a place where experienced contributors can mentor others and people new to contributing can find their footing without having to figure it out alone. It started when two of us ran into each other at the Boston Application Security Conference. Same organization, same department, had no idea the other was there. That conversation grew into three people, then a cross-regional group, and eventually an initiative with executive sponsorship built around a simple question: what if there was a structured space where people at all levels of OWASP engagement could come together, share what they know, coordinate where to show up, and help each other go deeper? That is what we built. A space where seasoned contributors have a home for their work and a way to pass it on, and where people curious about OWASP but not sure where to start can learn, get mentored, and take their first real steps. events.title: Gaelic Storm
events.description: It’s hard to imagine a band just coming into their own after 20 years of success, but that’s exactly what makes a true anomaly. Gaelic Storm, a multi-national, Celticjuggernaut grows stronger with each live performance, and after two decades and over 2000 shows, they are a true force to be reckoned with. The band attributes their continued success to their fanatic audience, and it’s a well-diversified crowd for sure – attracting fans of every genre with their richstorytelling, energetic instrumentals, devotion to Celtic traditions and passion for their stagecraft. They are as loyal to their fans as the fans are to them, as frontman Patrick Murphy states, “The fans are the ones that have given us this life. We’re here for them.” Gaelic Storm takes a true blue-collar, hard-nose approach to touring, consistently traveling the US and internationally forging a unique path in the Celtic musicworld. “You have to see us live. We are the true working-man’s’ band,” says longtime member Ryan Lacey. “We still, and most likely always will, tour most of theyear, and that’s how we constantly hone our craft.” This dedication to their live show dates all the way back to the mid-1990s, when Gaelic Storm kicked off its’ career as a pub band in Santa Monica, California. Onewhich performance led to their discovery that ultimately found the band appearing in the blockbuster film, Titanic (where they performed “Irish Party in ThirdClass”). This laid the groundwork for a career that would eventually find them topping the Billboard World Chart six times, making appearances at mainstreammusic festivals, and regularly headlining the largest Irish Festivals across the country, all while gaining a reputation as a genre-bending Irish rock band whosesongs mix Celtic traditions with something uniquely creative. Recent years have seen the addition of Natalya Kay on fiddle and Parker Hastings on guitar, who both bring their own energy, musicianship and spirit to GaelicStorm.

events.title: Gallery B Presents "Intersections | Realism & Abstraction"
events.description: “ INTERSECTIONS ⎸ Realism & Abstraction” is a group exhibition featuring four artists – Lawrence Chandler, Angela Iovino, Ariana Progri, and Ravi Raman - with distinct art styles in conversation with each other, showing that even the most realistic art is a form of abstraction (a reduction of reality) and that abstract art can hold elements of structural, grounded reality. Instead of treating realism and abstraction as binary opposites, works in the exhibition also intersect both worlds, showcasing how different artists navigate the spectrum between the two styles. Viewers not only will see realistic figures and recognizable subjects dissolving into, or emerging from abstract backgrounds, but also the use of bold brushstrokes, form, color, and textures to convey emotion rather than literal details. November 6, 2026 – November 29, 2026 Gallery Hours: Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays, 12 – 5pm Opening Reception: Friday, November 6; 6 – 9pm

events.title: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power
events.description: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power, an exhibition examining the beauty, dynamism, and political force of collective Black life across the African Diaspora through the photography of Howard alumna Adreinne Waheed. Curated by Kathryn Coney-Ali, executive director of the Howard University Gallery of Art, and Dr. Melanee C. Harvey-Fryar, associate professor of art history in the Chadwick A. Boseman College of Fine Arts, the exhibition brings Waheed’s documentary street photography into conversation with selections from the Waheed Photo Archive. Together, the works explore Black joy, protest, community, cultural tradition, and the power created when people gather. Necessary Means opens Wednesday, October 14, 2026, at the Howard University Museum in Founders Library and remains on view through May 28, 2027.

events.title: Research & Enrichment! Science with Your Dog
events.description: Join the GW Dog Lab for fun, free enrichment with your dog! The GW Canine Cognition Collaborative (aka GW Dog Lab) is a student-run lab in the Anthropology Department. Research sessions are on campus, after hours and on weekends, and are designed to last only 1 hour. Because humans and dogs share an environment, we can learn a lot about the way that environment has shaped our species by comparing dog and toddler cognition. We play simple games with dogs designed to measure their cognition and then compare them to toddlers. How to Participate 1. Start by submitting a pre-screening form. This helps us learn about your dog 2. Next, open your email and look for your onboarding information sent from canine.cognition@gwu.edu. 3. Then, using the information in your email, sign up for your initial visit. This is a get-to-know-you visit that makes it easier for dogs to get acclimated to our testing space. 4. Finally, after the initial visit, depending on your dog's comfort level, you will get email invitations to studies your dog is eligible for! Parking information can be found on the GW Dog Lab website.

events.title: Rockville Musical Theatre presents “Caroline, or Change”
events.description: 8 performances | Oct. 31 and Nov. 6*, 7, 13 & 14 at 7:30 p.m. | Nov. 1, 8 & 15 at 2 p.m. Set in one of the most pivotal times in America’s history, the Tony-nominated Caroline, or Change is riveting, moving, and awe-inspiring. Featuring a virtuosic score by Jeanine Tesori (Shrek The Musical, Thoroughly Modern Millie), it blends blues, gospel and traditional Jewish melodies, creating a breathtaking medium for Kushner’s provocative and personal story. In 1963, the Gellman family and their African-American maid, Caroline, live in sleepy Lake Charles, Louisiana. Caroline is drifting through life as a single mother of four, working in a service job for a white family. A fragile, yet beautiful friendship develops between the young Gellman son, Noah, and Caroline. Noah’s stepmother, Rose, unable to give Caroline a raise, tells Caroline that she may keep the money that Noah leaves in his pockets. Caroline balks and refuses to take money from a child, but her own children desperately need food, clothing and shoes. Outside of the laundry room, some of the greatest social advancements that the country has seen are being set in motion, and change is knocking on the door. Caroline, or Change, produces a valuable theatrical experience that continues to thrill audiences the world over. It is a story that must be shared and will touch hearts. events.title: Roots to Rest: AcuAroma Sleep Support with Ruxandra Meinze
events.address: 30 W. Potomac St., Ste 102, Brunswick, MD 21716
events.description: Step into a more intentional approach to rest with a 75-minute, hands-on AcuAroma Therapy workshop that brings together the therapeutic traditions of essential oils and Traditional Chinese Medicine acupressure. Working with a carefully selected collection of high-quality organic essential oils, you’ll be introduced to three specific oil and acupressure point pairings chosen to support relaxation and restorative sleep. Your facilitator will explore the therapeutic qualities of each oil, the significance of the corresponding organ points, and, most importantly, how these points relate to and work together as part of a larger practice. This is both a learning experience and a moment of self-pampering. You’ll have time to slow down, work with the oils directly, and learn a simple ritual you can return to whenever your body and mind need help transitioning into deeper rest. You’ll also leave with your own take-home collection of therapeutic oils, along with a laminated reference card featuring images of the three acupressure points so you can confidently locate and practice them at home. The goal is not simply to experience the work in the room, but to give you the knowledge, tools, and quality ingredients to make it part of your own evening ritual. No prior experience is needed. Come as you are, and leave with a deeper understanding of how aromatic medicine and acupressure can be thoughtfully combined to support your wellbeing.

events.title: Short Course: An Overview of LLMs for Statisticians: Foundations, Reasoning and Agentic AI
events.description: The GW Department of Statistics presents, An Overview of LLMs for Statisticians: Foundations, Reasoning, and Agentic AI, a short course taught by Linjun Zhang, associate professor in the Department of Statistics and an affiliated faculty member in computer science at Rutgers University Date/Time: November 6, 2026 9:00 a.m.–5:00 p.m. Lunch break: 12:00–1:30 p.m. Description: This short course provides an overview of the foundations and frontiers of modern large language models (LLMs), with an emphasis on topics relevant to statisticians and data scientists. We will begin with the basic principles underlying embeddings, transformers, and the LLM training pipeline, including pretraining, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from human feedback. Building on these foundations, we will discuss recent developments in reasoning models and agentic AI, including context engineering, harness engineering, and the design of AI agents for complex tasks. We will also discuss key issues in AI safety, reliability, and evaluation. The short course will combine conceptual foundations with practical examples and hands-on activities, with the goal of helping participants understand, use, and critically evaluate modern AI systems. Short Bio: Linjun Zhang is an Associate Professor in the Department of Statistics and an affiliated faculty member in Computer Science at Rutgers University. He received his Ph.D. in Statistics from the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylva

events.title: Unfossilizing African Art
events.description: Presented after extensive research, this exhibition recontextualizes African material culture objects held in the GW Collection for nearly 50 years. Led by Assistant Professor Clement Akpang, 59 students from four seminar courses offered between Fall 2024 and Spring 2026, conducted original research to deepen understanding of the university’s holdings and update how we interpret and exhibit these objects. The exhibition features 37 tangible heritage objects, ranging from an Egúngún Paaka from Yorubaland to a Kii [brass pipe], attributed to the Baumum people of Cameroon, accompanied by images and video that illuminate their rich histories. Research on the entire collection is presented in an accompanying illustrated publication. events.title: A Gift in Motion
events.description: A multidisciplinary showcase from the artists and scholars of the full-time faculty and staff at the Corcoran School of the Arts & Design. A Gift In Motion loosely draws from Robin Wall Kimmerer’s book The Serviceberry which uplifts Indigenous frameworks of the natural world to advance the possibilities in collectivity, reciprocity, and the mindset of abundance. These are anti-capitalist models and theories that provide insight into the systems of power we negotiate, but also offer a lens on how we individually move through our daily lives—together—through historically fraught landscapes. A keen reminder that working with, for, and because of each other remains the most human motivation, even while we are inundated with narratives that suggest otherwise. Within the walls of the academy, frameworks of artistic and creative knowledge are often dismissed, as are Indigenous methodologies and community-focused perspectives that center human engagement, oral and craft-based practices, and unquantifiable research. A personal experience. A feeling. Abstraction. And yet, for centuries, within the walls of art schools exist myriad economies of imagination that are anchored in the sharing of diverse creative knowledge and articulated in what we make, write, perform, dance, build, conserve, collect, display, speak, and think. events.title: Brady Art Gallery Tour: Unfossilizing African Art and Cracks & Reforms
events.description: Take a student-led tour of the exhibitions currently on view at the Brady Art Gallery: "Unfossilizing African Art" and "Cracks and Reforms". Unfossilizing African Art recontextualizes African material culture objects that have been held in the GW Collection for nearly 50 years. Led by Assistant Professor Clement Akpang, 59 students across four seminar courses conducted original research to deepen understanding of the collection and reconsider how these objects are interpreted and exhibited. Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection examines a decade shaped by political upheaval, social transformation, migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition. This exhibition, developed as part of an art history class taught by Associate Professor Bibi Obler, is accompanied by a catalog designed by graphic design students.

events.title: Camp One Heartland
events.description: Camp One Heartland is a solo exhibition by Tye DuSold-O’Connor archiving documentation of one of the world’s first nonprofit summer camps designated to supporting and empowering youth affected by HIV and AIDS, eventually transforming into a vital beacon of safety, liberation and eutopia for LGBTQ+ youth across the country. After its inaugural session in the summer of 1993 and many more held at different campsites across the country, Camp One Heartland found its permanent residence in Willow River, Minnesota. Over the next three decades it broadened its reach to provide summer camp sessions for youth experiencing housing instability, LGBTQ+ youth, and specifically trans youth. Tye attended Camp One Heartland as both a camper in 2022 and a counselor in 2024, and found these experiences indescribably transformative to them and their queer identity. Quite suddenly, Camp One Heartland shut down permanently in the fall of 2024 due to financial issues. Former campers, counselors and staff have been unable to return to the site since. While camp counseling in the summer of 2024, Tye took hundreds of photos of the camp, its people, and its experiences. These serve as some of the last images taken during the lifetime of Camp One Heartland. events.title: Cannupa Hanska Luger’s REFLECT
events.description: REFLECT traces the evolution of artist Cannuap Hanska Luger’s Mirror Shield Project. In 2016, when the Dakota Access Pipeline threatened the waters of his ancestral homelands, Luger circulated a video demonstrating how to make “mirror shields” from inexpensive materials. Conceived during the Indigenous-led resistance at Standing Rock, North Dakota, the tutorial functioned as a call to collective action, an invitation for people across the country to stand in solidarity with the Water Protectors. Carried by Water Protectors in frontline actions and collective formations, the mirrored surfaces offered protection while redirecting the field of vision. More than a thousand mirror shields were created and transported to the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ camp. The exhibition brings the project’s history into the present, treating the archive as a resource to be carried forward and put into practice. Photographs, videos, garments, ephemera, and community-generated documentation reveal a collective artwork shaped by those who made, carried, adapted, interpreted, and activated it.

events.title: Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection
events.description: The 1920s emerged as a decade suspended between collapse and reconstruction, an era marked by “cracks and reforms” that ushered in a profound reconfiguration of the visual world. During this period marked by civil transformation and political upheaval, artists, journalists, and makers had opportunities to reconstruct both individual and collective identities. A century later, Cracks & Reforms presents a distinct cross-section of this period, revealing global currents of migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition through the lens of the GW Collection. Students led by Associate Professor Bibiana Obler selected works to study and exhibit, their research eventually leading to unified themes and a catalog designed by Corcoran graphic design students led by professors Sharmila Karamchandani and Aasawari Kulkarni. Image: Boris Ignatovich (Russian, 1899-1976), Composer Dmitri Shostakovich, from "Ignatovich, Soviet Avant-Garde", 1928, gelatin silver print, 16 H x 20 W in. events.description: For Freedoms presents artist and educator Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY which centers on Ethiopian journalist and author Baalu Girma’s controversial 1984 Amharic novel Oromay, written under the Derg regime and banned shortly after its publication. Drawing on Gottesman’s deep engagement with the novel, NIGHT AND DAY considers how artists create, communicate, and sustain cultural memory within and against conditions of censorship, political repression, and state violence. These exhibitions are opening on Saturday, November 7 and can be viewed starting at 9 am. Beat the crowds and visit us earlier in the day! Nov 7–29 National Juried Photography Exhibition Part of FOCUS: A Celebration of Photography, the NJPE takes place every other year in November. The exhibition features selected photographs by regional and national artists. ABOUT THE JUROR: E. Brady Robinson is a Baltimore-based photographer and creative director known for her vibrant and eclectic mix of fine art photography, cultural documentation, and portraits of creatives. Her work has been featured in solo and group exhibitions in the US and internationally, and her photographs are held in the permanent collections of the Orlando Museum of Art and the Spanish Cultural Center in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic. Robinson teaches photography and senior seminar at Georgetown University and is a contributing photographer for BmoreArt and Baltimore Beat. Nov 7–29 Mark Seaver Beauty Through Thin Ice Photography Seaver’s photography uses ice and its properties as a filter through which to photograph. The result is the refraction of light, which distorts and abstracts the world seen through it. Nov 7–29 Christophe Casamassima The Dirty Window Photography The Dirty Window is a phantasmagoric cycle of photography that aligns with the four stages of sleep. Casamassima uses photography to explore how repetition reveals difference and where latent images surface to consciousness before dissolving again. Nov 7–29 Kevin Stivers Elsewhere Photography Elsewhere exists between places, neither here nor there. The work in Stiver’s exhibition explores themes of human connection and disconnect and feelings of belonging and misplacement, shrouded in a surreal atmosphere.

events.title: FACETED Seminar Series | Hand Sculpted: The Art & Evolution of Engraving
events.description: Join the InBloom team on Saturday, November 7th at 3PM in their Downtown Frederick gallery for the next talk in the FACETED seminar series— Hand Sculpted: The Art & Evolution of Engraving . A hand-engraved line isn’t simply applied to jewelry—it deliberately transforms the metal. For centuries, engravers have cut controlled lines into metal to preserve names, create intricate patterns, and bring surfaces and stories to life through texture, light, and shadow. It’s a beautiful expression of InBloom Jewelry’ philosophy: artistry in service to love. Whether a meaningful date inside a band, a name rendered in script, or a hand-cut design inspired by a personal story, hand engraving makes jewelry deeply personal and enduring—meticulously carved by a person, for a person (or by the InBloom goldsmiths, for you). This seminar will include a fascinating discussion on the history and evolution of hand engraving and a live demonstration of this centuries-old art form. Free to all, RSVPs encouraged.

events.title: From Grief to Becoming: A Guided Meditation for Identity Transitions with Danielle Kean Grassi
events.address: 30 W. Potomac St., Ste 102, Brunswick, MD 21716
events.description: Healing often brings an unexpected kind of grief. As you grow, you may notice yourself letting go of old roles, relationships, beliefs, or ways of coping that once helped you survive. While this transformation can be beautiful, it can also feel uncertain. This 90-minute guided meditation is a deeply reflective, primarily meditative experience designed to support you through that in-between space—not who you once were, but not yet fully who you're becoming. Through grounding practices, breath awareness, nervous system support, visualization, and gentle reflection, you'll be invited to notice what you're carrying, reconnect with your body's wisdom, and cultivate greater capacity for change with compassion. Because everyone's emotional experience is unique, participants are encouraged to move at their own pace. You're always welcome to pause, open your eyes, or simply observe if that feels most supportive. This offering is best suited for those navigating life transitions, personal growth, changing identities, or the emotional experience of becoming someone new. Feel free to bring along a journal and pen for reflection.

events.description: Protect the Health of YOUR Local Forest: Join us at Bacon Ridge Natural Area in Crownsville to spend a morning removing harmful invasive plants from along the trails! Scenic Rivers’ Healthy Forests Program engages community volunteers to help protect the long-term vitality of our largest conservation easement located within Bacon Ridge Natural Area. Our October 2026 workday will focus on vines, shrubs, and grasses. These aggressive invaders threaten vegetation at all levels of the forest from the ground up into the forest canopy. Event Details: Volunteers will be working on designated trail sections to remove specific invasive plant species. Volunteers will be trained in how to identify and remove these plants. Work gloves and tools can be provided by Scenic Rivers, though volunteers are welcome to bring their own gear. To participate, volunteers must: Be 16 years or older to attend without a supervising adult. Volunteers age 10 to 15 may attend with an accompanying adult(s) to supervise work; Be able to hike up to 1 mile to get to designated work areas. Wear long sleeve shirts, long pants, and closed toed shoes. Poison ivy is present in these work areas. Bring a full water bottle. We must have at least 5 registered volunteers for the workday to proceed. So, be sure to invite some friends! Controlling invasive species infestations is a big job and we’ll be happy to have as much help as possible!

events.title: Maryland Emancipation Day
events.address: 8000 Walker Mill Road, Capitol Heights, MD 20743
events.description: What We Carried into Freedom: Knowledge • Skill • Culture • Community Join us at Concord Historic Site for the Maryland Emancipation Day Celebration, an afternoon of living history, music, storytelling, food, family, and community as we commemorate the abolition of slavery in Maryland. Maryland’s Constitution of 1864 took effect on November 1, ending slavery in the state and freeing more than 30,000 African Americans. At Concord—a former tobacco plantation where generations of African Americans were enslaved—Emancipation Day offers an opportunity to remember that history while exploring what freedom made possible. Throughout the afternoon, discover the skills, knowledge, creativity, and cultural traditions African Americans carried through enslavement and used to build lives, families, businesses, institutions, and communities after emancipation. A Celebration Rooted in History Craft Demonstration Area Meet skilled artisans and tradition bearers demonstrating historic and contemporary crafts while discovering the knowledge, creativity, and craftsmanship behind their work. The Griot Sound Stage Experience the power of African American music, storytelling, spoken word, and performance. Inspired by the African tradition of the griot as a keeper of history and community memory, the stage brings stories of culture, freedom, and resilience to life. Hands-On History: Community Glass Project Leave your mark on Concord’s story. Participate in a special, hands-on glass activity connected to the artwork being created for the historic site and learn how community voices are becoming part of Concord’s evolving interpretation. Food Pavilion Take a break, gather around the table, and enjoy food available from participating vendors throughout the celebration.

events.title: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power
events.description: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power, an exhibition examining the beauty, dynamism, and political force of collective Black life across the African Diaspora through the photography of Howard alumna Adreinne Waheed. Curated by Kathryn Coney-Ali, executive director of the Howard University Gallery of Art, and Dr. Melanee C. Harvey-Fryar, associate professor of art history in the Chadwick A. Boseman College of Fine Arts, the exhibition brings Waheed’s documentary street photography into conversation with selections from the Waheed Photo Archive. Together, the works explore Black joy, protest, community, cultural tradition, and the power created when people gather. Necessary Means opens Wednesday, October 14, 2026, at the Howard University Museum in Founders Library and remains on view through May 28, 2027.
